name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q01 - Types of movement and muscle properties

questiontext.text:
Read the following four statements regarding types of movement and muscular tissue in humans:

Statement I: Macrophages and leucocytes in blood exhibit amoeboid movement effected by pseudopodia and cytoskeletal microfilaments.

Statement II: Ciliary movement facilitates the passage of ova through the female reproductive tract and removes dust particles from the trachea.

Statement III: Visceral muscles line hollow internal organs, lack striations, and are under voluntary control of the nervous system.

Statement IV: Cardiac muscle cells assemble in a branching pattern, appear striated, and are involuntary in nature.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Human cells exhibit amoeboid, ciliary, and muscular movements, while human muscular tissues are classified into skeletal, visceral (smooth), and cardiac types based on location, striations, and nervous regulation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Propositions
The proposition that macrophages and leucocytes exhibit amoeboid movement via pseudopodia and microfilaments is accurate. The proposition that ciliary movement in ciliated epithelium clears dust from the trachea and assists ova transport through the female reproductive tract is also accurate. However, visceral (smooth) muscles located in the inner walls of hollow visceral organs are not under voluntary control of the nervous system; they are involuntary muscles, making that claim incorrect. Finally, cardiac muscle cells assemble in a branching pattern, display striations, and are involuntary in nature, which is accurate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The propositions describing amoeboid movement in blood cells, ciliary movement in the trachea and female reproductive tract, and branched involuntary striated cardiac muscles are correct, whereas the claim that visceral muscles are voluntary is incorrect.

answer.text: All four statements (I, II, III, and IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q02 - Disorders of muscular and skeletal system

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements regarding disorders of the muscular and skeletal system:

Statement I: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction, leading to fatigue, weakening, and paralysis of skeletal muscle.

Statement II: Muscular dystrophy is a progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle mostly due to a genetic disorder.

Statement III: Tetany is characterised by rapid spasms in muscle due to low \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) in body fluid.

Statement IV: Osteoporosis is an age-related disorder characterised by increased bone mass due to elevated levels of estrogen.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Disorders of the muscular and skeletal system stem from autoimmune attack, genetic mutations, ionic imbalances, hormonal declines, or metabolic crystal deposition.

Step 2: Evaluation of Propositions
Myasthenia gravis is accurately described as an autoimmune disorder targeting the neuromuscular junction and causing fatigue, weakening, and paralysis of skeletal muscle. Muscular dystrophy is accurately described as progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle mostly caused by a genetic disorder. Tetany is accurately described as rapid, wild muscle spasms caused by low \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) levels in body fluid. In contrast, osteoporosis is an age-related disorder characterised by decreased bone mass and increased fracture risk, commonly caused by decreased (not elevated) levels of estrogen.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The descriptions of myasthenia gravis, muscular dystrophy, and tetany are correct, whereas the claim that osteoporosis involves increased bone mass and elevated estrogen is incorrect.

answer.text: All four statements (I, II, III, and IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q03 - Skeletal muscle fibre and sarcomere structure

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements regarding the ultrastructure of a skeletal muscle:

Statement I: Muscle bundles (fascicles) in a skeletal muscle are held together by a common collagenous connective tissue layer called fascia.

Statement II: A muscle fibre is a syncitium because its sarcoplasm contains many nuclei, and its sarcoplasmic reticulum stores \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) ions.

Statement III: The portion of a myofibril between two successive M-lines is considered the functional unit of contraction called a sarcomere.

Statement IV: In a resting state, the central part of the thick filament not overlapped by thin filaments is called the H-zone.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A skeletal muscle is organised into fascicles wrapped by fascia, containing multinucleated muscle fibres with parallel myofibrils divided into repeating contractile units called sarcomeres.

Step 2: Evaluation of Propositions
Fascicles are held together by a common collagenous connective tissue layer called fascia, which is accurate. A muscle fibre is indeed a syncitium containing many nuclei in the sarcoplasm, and its sarcoplasmic reticulum acts as the storehouse of calcium ions, which is accurate. However, the sarcomere (functional unit of contraction) is defined as the portion of the myofibril between two successive Z-lines—not M-lines (the M-line is the thin fibrous membrane holding thick filaments in the middle of the A-band). Finally, in the resting state, the central part of the thick filament not overlapped by thin filaments is accurately termed the H-zone.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding fascia, the syncitial muscle fibre with calcium-storing sarcoplasmic reticulum, and the H-zone are correct, whereas defining a sarcomere as the region between two successive M-lines instead of Z-lines is incorrect.

answer.text: All four statements (I, II, III, and IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q04 - Structure of actin and myosin contractile proteins

questiontext.text:
Read the following four statements regarding the contractile proteins actin and myosin:

Statement I: Each actin filament consists of two helically wound F-actin strands, each being a polymer of monomeric G-actins.

Statement II: Two filaments of tropomyosin run close to the F-actins throughout their length, with troponin distributed at regular intervals on tropomyosin.

Statement III: In the resting state, a subunit of troponin masks the active binding sites for myosin on the actin filaments.

Statement IV: The heavy meromyosin (HMM) component of meromyosin projects outwards as the cross arm and its globular head is an active ATPase enzyme.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Muscle contraction depends on the molecular architecture of thin filaments (F-actin, tropomyosin, troponin) and thick filaments (polymerised meromyosins divided into HMM and LMM).

Step 2: Evaluation of Propositions
Each thin actin filament is composed of two F-actin chains helically wound around each other, where each F-actin is a polymer of monomeric G-actin units; this is accurate. Two tropomyosin filaments run close to F-actins along their length, and the complex protein troponin is distributed at regular intervals on tropomyosin; this is accurate. In the resting state, a subunit of troponin masks the myosin-binding active sites on actin filaments; this is also accurate. Finally, the HMM component (globular head with short arm) projects outwards from the thick filament surface as the cross arm, and the globular head functions as an active ATPase enzyme with ATP-binding and actin-binding sites; this is accurate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
All four propositions describing F-actin/G-actin polymerisation, tropomyosin and troponin arrangement, resting-state masking of actin by troponin, and the HMM cross arm with its ATPase globular head are correct.

answer.text: All four statements (I, II, III, and IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q05 - Mechanism of contraction and muscle fibre types

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements regarding the mechanism of muscle contraction and fibre types:

Statement I: A neural signal reaching the neuromuscular junction releases acetylcholine, generating an action potential in the sarcolemma that triggers \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) release into the sarcoplasm.

Statement II: During contraction, the I-bands get reduced in length, whereas the A-bands retain their length.

Statement III: Red fibres contain high myoglobin and plenty of mitochondria, making them aerobic muscles.

Statement IV: White fibres possess high myoglobin content, abundant mitochondria, and very little sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Neural excitation at the motor-end plate triggers sarcoplasmic \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) release and sliding of thin filaments over thick filaments, while skeletal muscle fibres differ in myoglobin, mitochondrial density, and sarcoplasmic reticulum abundance.

Step 2: Evaluation of Propositions
Arrival of a neural signal at the neuromuscular junction releases acetylcholine, generating a sarcolemmal action potential that causes \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) release into the sarcoplasm; this is accurate. During sarcomere shortening, thin filaments slide inward, reducing I-band length while the A-band retains its constant length; this is accurate. Red fibres have high oxygen-storing myoglobin and numerous mitochondria for aerobic ATP production, making them aerobic muscles; this is accurate. However, White fibres actually have very less myoglobin, few mitochondria, and a high amount of sarcoplasmic reticulum, relying on anaerobic processes for energy—the opposite of what is claimed.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding acetylcholine-mediated \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) release, I-band reduction with constant A-band length, and aerobic Red fibres are correct, whereas the description of White fibres as myoglobin-rich with low sarcoplasmic reticulum is incorrect.

answer.text: All four statements (I, II, III, and IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q06 - Axial skeleton skull, vertebrae, and ribs

questiontext.text:
Read the following four statements regarding the human axial skeleton:

Statement I: The skull has 22 cranial and facial bones (8 cranial and 14 facial), along with a single U-shaped hyoid bone and 6 ear ossicles in total.

Statement II: The human skull is dicondylic, articulating with the first vertebra (atlas) via two occipital condyles.

Statement III: Each rib is bicephalic because it has two articulation surfaces on its dorsal end.

Statement IV: The 8th, 9th, and 10th pairs of ribs are called floating ribs because they are not connected ventrally.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The axial skeleton (80 bones) comprises the skull, vertebral column, sternum, and 12 pairs of ribs, each with specific counts and articulation patterns.

Step 2: Evaluation of Propositions
The skull includes 8 cranial and 14 facial bones (total 22), a single U-shaped hyoid bone at the base of the buccal cavity, and 3 ear ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) in each middle ear (\(3 \times 2 = 6\) total), making the first proposition accurate. The skull articulates with the superior region of the vertebral column (atlas) via two occipital condyles (dicondylic skull), making the second proposition accurate. Each rib has two articulation surfaces on its dorsal end and is therefore called bicephalic, making the third proposition accurate. However, the 8th, 9th, and 10th pairs of ribs join the seventh rib via hyaline cartilage and are called vertebrochondral (false) ribs; it is the last two pairs (11th and 12th) that lack ventral connections and are called floating ribs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding skull bone counts, dicondylic articulation with the atlas, and bicephalic ribs are correct, whereas classifying the 8th, 9th, and 10th rib pairs as floating ribs is incorrect.

answer.text: All four statements (I, II, III, and IV)

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements regarding the human appendicular skeleton:

Statement I: Each forelimb has 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, and 14 phalanges, whereas each hindlimb has 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, and 14 phalanges.

Statement II: The scapula is situated in the dorsal part of the thorax between the second and the seventh ribs, and its acromion process articulates with the clavicle.

Statement III: Each coxal bone of the pelvic girdle is formed by the fusion of ilium, ischium, and pubis, with the glenoid cavity at their point of fusion.

Statement IV: The two halves of the pelvic girdle meet ventrally to form the pubic symphysis containing fibrous cartilage.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The appendicular skeleton consists of the limb bones (30 per limb) and the pectoral and pelvic girdles that articulate the upper and lower limbs with the axial skeleton.

Step 2: Evaluation of Propositions
The forelimb wrist/palm/digit counts (8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges) and hindlimb ankle/sole/digit counts (7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges) are accurate, summing with the long bones (and patella in the leg) to 30 bones per limb. The scapula lies dorsally between the 2nd and 7th ribs, and its spine projects as the flat, expanded acromion process with which the clavicle articulates; this is accurate. However, at the point of fusion of ilium, ischium, and pubis in each coxal bone lies the acetabulum (for articulation with the femur), whereas the glenoid cavity belongs to the scapula of the pectoral girdle (for articulation with the humerus); thus assigning the glenoid cavity to the coxal bone is incorrect. Finally, the two pelvic halves meet ventrally at the pubic symphysis containing fibrous cartilage, which is accurate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The propositions detailing limb bone counts, scapular location and acromion-clavicle articulation, and the fibrous-cartilage pubic symphysis are correct, whereas placing the glenoid cavity in the coxal bone instead of the acetabulum is incorrect.

answer.text: All four statements (I, II, III, and IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q08 - Classification and examples of human joints

questiontext.text:
Analyse the following four statements regarding joints in the human skeletal system:

Statement I: Fibrous joints, shown by flat skull bones fusing end-to-end as sutures, do not allow any movement.

Statement II: Cartilaginous joints between adjacent vertebrae in the vertebral column permit limited movements.

Statement III: Synovial joints possess a fluid-filled synovial cavity between articulating bone surfaces, allowing considerable movement.

Statement IV: Ball and socket joint (humerus and pectoral girdle), pivot joint (atlas and axis), and saddle joint (carpal and metacarpal of thumb) are all types of synovial joints.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Joints are points of contact between bones or between bones and cartilages that act as fulcrums for muscular force, classified structurally into fibrous, cartilaginous, and synovial joints.

Step 2: Evaluation of Propositions
Flat skull bones fuse end-to-end with dense fibrous connective tissues in the form of sutures, forming fibrous joints that allow no movement; this is accurate. Adjacent vertebrae are joined by cartilage, forming cartilaginous joints that permit limited movements; this is accurate. Synovial joints feature a fluid-filled synovial cavity between articulating surfaces, enabling considerable movement for locomotion and other actions; this is accurate. Furthermore, the ball and socket joint (between humerus and pectoral girdle), pivot joint (between atlas and axis), and saddle joint (between carpal and metacarpal of thumb), along with hinge and gliding joints, are all examples of synovial joints; this is accurate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
All four propositions—concerning immovable fibrous sutures, limited-movement cartilaginous intervertebral joints, fluid-filled synovial cavities, and the listed synovial joint examples—are correct.

answer.text: All four statements (I, II, III, and IV)
